title: The Impact of Common Myopia Interventions on Quality of Life: A Cost-Effectiveness Analysis.
journal: Ophthalmic & physiological optics : the journal of the British College of Ophthalmic Opticians (Optometrists)
first_affiliation: National Clinical Research Center for Ocular Diseases, Eye Hospital, Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, China.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of multiple myopia control interventions in managing myopia progression from a quality-of-life perspective.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A Markov cohort model simulated myopia progression over 10 years in children starting treatment at 8 years of age. Cost-effectiveness was evaluated using the incremental cost-utility ratio (ICUR) and incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), measured as cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained and cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted, respectively. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses assessed model robustness. If an intervention exhibited sensitivity or instability, its cost-effectiveness cannot be determined conclusively within the range of parameter variations.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: In the QALY analysis, outdoor activity was strongly dominant (ICUR: CN ￥-2641 [US $-371] per QALY). Highly aspherical lenslet spectacles (HALs) showed the most favourable ICUR among remaining interventions (CN ￥114,809 [US $16,125]). Based on the expected values, all interventions except multifocal soft contact lenses (MSCLs), rigid gas permeable contact lenses (RGPCLs) and orthokeratology (OK) demonstrated cost‑effectiveness. However, the results for bifocal spectacle lenses (BSLs), progressive addition lenses and red‑light therapy exhibited instability. In the DALY analysis, outdoor activity remained dominant (saving CN ￥7953 [US $1117] per DALY averted). The expected value analysis revealed that outdoor activity and BSLs were the only cost-effective interventions. Meanwhile, bifocal and progressive addition spectacles and HALs showed sensitivity.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: From a QALY perspective, outdoor activity, 0.01% atropine and myopia-control spectacle lenses, excluding contact lenses and those with volatile results, were cost-effective, with outdoor activity being dominant and HALs being the most favourable alternative. Using DALYs, only outdoor activity was stably cost-effective, indicating more conservative conclusions.

title: Red Light Therapy and Mitochondrial Rejuvenation in Age-Related Disorders.
first_affiliation: The Student Scientific Society, Poznan University of Medical Sciences, 60-806, Poznan, Poland.

abstract.text: Aging is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired ATP production, and a decline in tissue regenerative capacity, leading to the development of age-related diseases. This review summarizes current evidence regarding the effects of photobiomodulation (PBM) on mitochondrial function and age-related disorders. PBM using red and near-infrared light may enhance proper mitochondrial function by acting on cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) and other signaling pathways, including the transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) channel, leading to increased ATP production, modulation of ROS signaling, and improved cellular homeostasis. We review in vitro, animal, and clinical studies investigating PBM in metabolic, neurodegenerative, hepatic, cardiovascular, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), and skeletal muscle disorders associated with aging, as well as its application in the management of cancer therapy-related oral mucositis. Current studies demonstrate beneficial effects on glucose metabolism, cardiovascular function, neuronal function, lipid metabolism, liver function, muscle regeneration, and visual function in AMD, as well as the safety and efficacy of PBM in the management of cancer therapy-induced oral mucositis. The therapeutic effects of PBM appear to be dose-dependent and influenced by treatment parameters including wavelength, fluence, irradiance, and exposure protocol. Although photobiomodulation still lacks standardized treatment protocols and differences exist in the wavelengths used, dosage, and frequency among studies, it represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of age-related diseases.

title: Atropine, red-light therapy, and lenslet spectacles for premyopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
journal: Graefe's archive for clinical and experimental ophthalmology = Albrecht von Graefes Archiv fur klinische und experimentelle Ophthalmologie
first_affiliation: Applied Physics Department (Optometry Area), Facultade de Óptica e Optometría, Universidade de Santiago de Compostela, Santiago de Compostela, 15705, Spain. claramartinez.perez@usc.es.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Earlier onset of childhood myopia is associated with greater subsequent progression and a higher risk of high myopia and related ocular complications. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether low-concentration atropine, repeated low-level red-light therapy (RLRL), and study-specific lenslet-array spectacle designs reduce refractive change and axial elongation in non-myopic children classified as premyopic.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251252431) and conducted according to PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to 17 July 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials with follow-up ranging from 3 to 24 months that included children meeting study-specific criteria for premyopia and reported cycloplegic spherical equivalent (SE) and/or axial length (AL). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using GRADE. Mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using RevMan 11.4.2.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Eight randomized controlled trials were included, seven conducted in China and one in India. At 12 months, 0.01% atropine was associated with a smaller myopic shift in SE (4 studies; 574 participants; MD, + 0.32 D; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.52; I² = 72%; low-certainty evidence). RLRL also favored a smaller myopic shift (2 studies; 307 participants; MD, + 0.38 D; 95% CI, - 0.05 to 0.81; I² = 0%; very-low-certainty evidence). One study-specific positive Lenslet-Array-Integrated spectacle design involving 173 participants reported an MD of + 0.45 D (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.52). For AL, atropine showed a trend toward reduced axial elongation (MD, - 0.13 mm; 95% CI, - 0.26 to - 0.00; I² = 74%; very-low-certainty evidence), whereas RLRL showed an MD of - 0.16 mm (95% CI, - 0.30 to - 0.01; I² = 0%; very-low-certainty evidence). The lenslet-array study reported an MD of - 0.31 mm (95% CI, - 0.42 to - 0.20). Technical reporting and adverse-event assessment were incomplete, particularly for optical and red-light interventions.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Available randomized evidence suggests that some interventions may reduce early refractive change in children classified as premyopic, while effects on axial elongation remain less certain. Atropine had the largest evidence base, but certainty was low for SE and very low for AL. RLRL and the study-specific lenslet-array spectacle design showed potential benefits; however, limited replication, incomplete technical characterization, restricted geographic representation, and insufficient long-term safety evidence limit confidence and generalizability.

title: Red and near-infrared photobiomodulation in precision medicine: mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation.
first_affiliation: Medical Equipment Department, Affiliated Hospital of Jining Medical University, Jining, Shandong, China.

abstract.text: Phototherapy is a non-invasive therapeutic modality that uses specific wavelengths of light to modulate biological processes and treat disease. Driven by advances in photobiology, regenerative medicine, and clinical technology, phototherapy has evolved from empirical heliotherapy into a mechanism-based intervention with expanding medical applications. This review places the biological effects, therapeutic indications, and safety profiles of ultraviolet, blue, and green light in comparative context, while focusing primarily on the mechanisms, dosimetry, and clinical translation of red and near-infrared photobiomodulation (PBM). Although ultraviolet and blue light therapies have established roles in dermatology and neonatal jaundice, their clinical use is limited by concerns such as photocarcinogenesis, retinal phototoxicity, and circadian disruption. In contrast, red and near-infrared light offer deeper tissue penetration and, when appropriately dosed, a comparatively low risk of direct photochemical injury. Through mitochondrial, redox, inflammatory, and other context-dependent signaling pathways, red/NIR PBM has been investigated in wound repair, chronic pain, osteoarthritis, musculoskeletal disorders, neurological conditions, and dermatological applications. As a representative quantitative example, a 2024 meta-analysis of 10 placebo-controlled randomized trials involving 542 participants with knee osteoarthritis found a moderate reduction in pain at rest with PBM compared with placebo (standardized mean difference, - 0.70; 95% confidence interval, - 1.10 to - 0.20), although the certainty of evidence was very low. However, broader clinical translation remains constrained by heterogeneous dosimetry, insufficiently standardized treatment protocols, and uneven evidence maturity across indications. To address these limitations, we propose a precision-oriented framework that links clinical target, tissue-optical context, wavelength selection, patient- and site-specific modifiers, dosimetric implications, measurable endpoints, and evidence maturity. This framework is intended to support treatment planning, parameter reporting, and prospective validation rather than to prescribe currently validated individualized dosing algorithms.

title: Effects of myopia control interventions on myopia progression and strabismus-related outcomes in children with intermittent exotropia: a systematic review and meta-analysis protocol.
first_affiliation: Department of Ophthalmology, Shanxi Eye Hospital Affiliated to Shanxi Medical University, Taiyuan, Shanxi, China.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Intermittent exotropia frequently coexists with childhood myopia. Myopia-control interventions may affect accommodation, convergence or binocular function but evidence specific to children with intermittent exotropia has not been synthesised. This review will assess efficacy in randomised trials and comparative effectiveness and safety in non-randomised studies considering both myopia progression and strabismus-related outcomes.

abstract.label: METHODS AND ANALYSIS
abstract.text: This protocol follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) 2015 statement. We will search PubMed, Embase (Elsevier), Web of Science Core Collection, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, Wanfang Data and VIP Database together with ClinicalTrials.gov and the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry from inception to the final search date. The final searches are planned for May 2027. Eligible reports will include randomised trials and non-randomised comparative studies of participants aged 18 years or younger with intermittent exotropia and myopia. Interventions will include low-concentration atropine, orthokeratology, myopia-control spectacle lenses, repeated low-level red-light therapy and relevant combination regimens. Primary outcomes are changes in spherical equivalent refraction, axial length and distance and near angles of deviation. Two reviewers will independently select studies, extract data and assess risk of bias using RoB 2 for randomised trials and Risk Of Bias In Non-randomized Studies- of Interventions (ROBINS-I) for non-randomised studies. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach will be used to assess certainty of evidence. Meta-analysis will be restricted to studies with comparable intervention technologies, study designs, comparators, outcome definitions and follow-up periods; otherwise, findings will be synthesised narratively.

abstract.label: ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION
abstract.text: Ethics approval is not required because only published and publicly available data will be used. Findings will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal and presented at scientific meetings.

title: Axial Length Stabilization and Scleral Curvature Changes following Repeated Low-level Red-light Therapy in Children with High Myopia.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: To determine the incidence and extent of axial length (AL) shortening after 12 months of repeated low-level red-light (RLRL) therapy in highly myopic eyes. In addition, to investigate the relationship between the AL shortening and changes in the posterior scleral curvature in the swept-source optical coherence tomographic (SS-OCT) images.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Thirty participants aged 8 to 18 years with high myopia were studied. The spherical equivalent of refractive error (SER) and AL were measured, and SS-OCT images were recorded at baseline, and at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after beginning RLRL therapy.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Twelve months of RLRL therapy led to an average reduction in myopic SER by 0.29 D (95% CI, 0.10 to 0.49 D; P < 0.05) and stabilization of AL, with a mean change of -0.03 mm (95% CI, -0.09 to 0.04 mm; P = 1.00). AL shortening >0.05 mm was observed in 53.8% of eyes. The average increase in the macular choroidal thickness was 26 µm (95% CI, 20 to 32 µm; P < 0.05), and an apparent change in posterior scleral curvature was observed in 5/26 (19.2%) eyes. One participant discontinued the RLRL therapy on day 2 because of photophobia. None of the other participants reported persistent photophobia or afterimage throughout the study, but one had 2 line reduction in BCVA without any OCT structural change.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: RLRL therapy was associated with AL stabilization in highly myopic eyes. Although apparent scleral curvature change was observed, it was a post hoc analysis in a small number of eyes and its association with choroidal thickness and the shortening of the AL needs further investigation.

title: Cost-effectiveness of monotherapy and combination therapy for myopia control in Chinese children.
first_affiliation: Tianjin Key Laboratory of Retinal Functions and Diseases, Tianjin Branch of National Clinical Research Center for Ocular Disease, Eye Institute and School of Optometry, Tianjin Medical University Eye Hospital, Tianjin, China.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Myopia poses a major public health and economic burden in China, necessitating cost-effectiveness evaluations of control strategies. We aimed to assess cost-effectiveness of single/combined myopia control in children and adolescents to optimise strategies.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: We conducted a network meta-analysis to evaluate the efficacy of myopia control interventions in Chinese children (aged 6-18 years). Annual changes in axial length (AL) and spherical equivalent refraction (SER) were the primary outcomes. Additionally, we used a decision-analytic Markov model with clinical and cost data from China to evaluate 16 myopia control strategies for eight-year-old children over eight years from a patient perspective, with 3% discounting. Strategies included monotherapies and combined therapies. Main outcomes were incremental cost per unit reduction in myopic shift (i.e. SER) or AL elongation, compared with single-vision lenses (SVLs). Markov cohort analysis simulated the proportion of individuals progressing to high myopia under various strategies. We assessed robustness through deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses. We performed subgroup analyses by onset age (6, 10, and 12 years) and regional economic development.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: For SER reduction, outdoor activity was cost-effective (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = USD -18.29/dioptre (D)). At higher willingness-to-pay thresholds, 0.01% atropine combined with defocus incorporated multiple segment (DIMS) (USD 660.74/D) and repeated low-level red-light therapy (RLRL) (USD 895.36/D) were cost-effective. For AL reduction, outdoor activity (USD -42.68/mm) and DIMS (USD 672.73/mm) were cost-effective at lower thresholds, while RLRL (USD 2011.32/mm) was preferred at higher thresholds. Compared with monotherapy, combination interventions improved preventive efficacy against high myopia. Subgroup analyses confirmed that the cost-effectiveness ranking was preserved across onset ages and regional economic settings.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Under limited budget conditions, outdoor activities and defocus spectacles represent advantageous cost-effective treatment options. When the budget is sufficient, RLRL may be considered a promising option pending confirmation of its long-term safety and effectiveness, and 0.01% atropine combined with DIMS is the preferred cost-effective option. Our analysis provides evidence-based guidance for clinicians and families in selecting effective myopia control strategies.

title: Transcranial Photobiomodulation Attenuates Neurogenic Inflammation and Sensory Hypersensitivity in a Nitroglycerin-Induced Migraine Model: Toward a Nonpharmacological Therapy.
first_affiliation: Neurosciences Research Center, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz, Iran, tbzmed.ac.ir.

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Migraine is a debilitating neurological condition, characterized by headache, photophobia, and heightened mechanical/thermal sensitivity. Current pharmacological therapies often lead to incomplete relief and adverse effects, necessitating the use of noninvasive alternatives. This study evaluated transcranial photobiomodulation (PBM) in a nitroglycerin (NTG)-induced migraine model in male mice.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Mice were assigned to Sham, NTG, NTG + Sumatriptan (SUMA; 600 µg/kg, s.c.), NTG + PBM, and NTG + PBM + SUMA groups. Over 9 days, NTG (5 mg/kg) was injected intraperitoneally every other day to develop an animal model of chronic migraine. The PBM protocol involved daily irradiation (810 nm) on the occipital bone of the head for 5 s over 9 days. The animals underwent behavioral testing for photophobia, mechanical allodynia, and thermal sensitivity. The trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) was assessed for miR-155 expression by real-time PCR and protein expression of phospho-NF-κB, IL-1β, transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) and vanilloid 1 (TRPV1), calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), c-Fos, and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) using immunoblotting.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Behavioral assessment revealed that PBM significantly reduced head scratching and improved exploratory activity, decreased light aversion, reversed periorbital/hindpaw mechanical allodynia, and prolonged thermal withdrawal latency compared to the NTG group. Moreover, PBM downregulated miR-155 expression and decreased levels of inflammatory mediators and migraine-associated neuropeptides in the TNC. Notably, combined PBM and SUMA treatment resulted in improvements in behavioral and molecular outcomes compared to either treatment alone.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: These results indicate that PBM inhibited migraine-like behaviors and decreased the expression of numerous molecular markers that are linked to neuroinflammation and trigeminal activation in the TNC. These findings establish a foundation for additional research on transcranial PBM as a noninvasive method for modulating migraine-related behavioral responses.

title: Effects of Repeated Low-Level Red-Light Therapy on Subfoveal Choroidal Thickness in Children with Myopia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
first_affiliation: Department of Ophthalmology, Taichung Veterans General Hospital, Taichung 407, Taiwan.

abstract.text: Background/Objectives: Repeated low-level red-light (RLRL) therapy has recently emerged as a promising treatment for childhood myopia. Choroidal thickening has been proposed as a key biological mechanism underlying its therapeutic efficacy; however, evidence regarding its effects on subfoveal choroidal thickness (SFCT), particularly in children with premyopia, remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate the effects of RLRL therapy on SFCT in pediatric patients with myopia and premyopia. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were systematically searched from database inception through 29 September 2026. Randomized controlled trials comparing RLRL therapy with controls in participants younger than 18 years were included. The primary outcome was the change in SFCT at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12 months. Mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted according to refractive status. Results: Thirteen randomized controlled trials comprising 1974 children were included. In children with myopia, RLRL therapy was associated with significantly greater increases in SFCT than the control across all follow-up time points, with the greatest mean difference observed at 9 months (MD = 37.01 μm, 95% CI, 30.48-43.54). In children with premyopia, RLRL therapy also induced significant SFCT thickening from 1 to 9 months. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings, and no evidence of significant publication bias was identified. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate consistent choroidal thickening following RLRL therapy in children with myopia and premyopia and support further investigation into the potential role of choroidal changes in myopia control.

title: Addressing the need for improved safety monitoring of red light therapy for myopia control in children.
journal: Optometry and vision science : official publication of the American Academy of Optometry
first_affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, School of Engineering Sciences, AlbaNova, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH), Stockholm, Sweden.

title: Low-level light therapy for dry eye disease and meibomian gland dysfunction: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
first_affiliation: Department of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Oslo University Hospital, Oslo, Norway.

abstract.text: A healthy tear film is vital for ocular surface integrity and relies on the coordinated function of the lacrimal glands, meibomian glands and conjunctival goblet cells. Dysfunction in any of these elements can lead to dry eye disease (DED). This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the efficacy of low-level light therapy (LLLT) as a standalone DED treatment. Although evidence for LLLT's therapeutic potential is growing, prior reviews have focused on short-term outcomes or combined LLLT with intense pulsed light. This meta-analysis consolidates current findings to clarify the clinical value of LLLT monotherapy in DED management. We systematically searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for studies evaluating LLLT for DED. Study selection and data extraction were conducted according to pre-specified inclusion and exclusion criteria. Meta-analyses were performed for Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI), non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT) and tear meniscus height (TMH). Ten clinical studies were eligible for our systematic review, which included a total of 473 participants. Irradiation protocols included treatment sessions using wavelengths of 625-640 nm and/or 810-850 nm, with each session lasting a minimum of 10 min. In our meta-analyses, LLLT monotherapy was associated with significant improvements in OSDI (weighted mean difference [WMD] -11.42, p < 0.00001), NIBUT (WMD +1.49 s, p = 0.005), and TMH (WMD +0.04 mm, p = 0.007). Sensitivity analyses restricted to eligible RCTs confirmed significant effects on OSDI and NIBUT, but not on TMH. No adverse events were reported. LLLT appears to be well tolerated and may improve signs and symptoms of DED, particularly ocular discomfort. It may represent a promising standalone treatment option for patients in whom combination regimens involving IPL treatment are contraindicated.

title: Intense pulsed light as a multi-target intervention paradigm for refractory ocular surface diseases: a review.
first_affiliation: National Clinical Research Center for Ocular Diseases, Eye Hospital, Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, 325027, China.

abstract.text: Ocular surface diseases (OSDs) are a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by overlapping inflammatory, vascular, microbial, neuroimmune, and meibomian gland abnormalities that contribute to the onset and persistence of ocular surface symptoms and signs. Conventional symptom-directed therapies do not adequately alleviate refractory meibomian gland dysfunction, Demodex-associated blepharitis, ocular rosacea, recurrent chalazion, and allergic conjunctivitis. Recent evidence suggests that these conditions may share convergent pathological features, including chronic inflammation, abnormal lid-margin vascularity, and microbial or parasitic imbalance. Intense pulsed light (IPL), which was initially used for vascular and inflammatory disorders in dermatology, has emerged as a potential physical therapy that acts through several proposed mechanisms in patients with selected refractory OSDs, including photothermal liquefaction of inspissated meibum, coagulation of abnormal vessels, reduction of Demodex and microbial burden, modulation of inflammatory responses, and possible effects on neuroimmune signaling; however, these mechanisms remain incompletely established. Case series and clinical studies have reported improvements in ocular symptoms, tear film stability, meibomian gland function and drainage, lid-margin inflammation, and chalazion or lesion resolution, particularly when IPL is combined with meibomian gland expression or other adjunctive therapies. However, treatment responses vary across disease phenotypes and standardized treatment parameters, long-term safety data, and high-quality randomized controlled trials remain limited. Anatomical factors, disease severity, glandular structure, and inflammatory status may also influence therapeutic outcomes. Overall, IPL therapy represents a promising but evolving treatment strategy for refractory OSDs. This review summarizes the current knowledge regarding the proposed mechanisms, clinical applications, treatment protocols, limitations, and future directions and provides updated perspectives for the rational use of IPL in OSD management.

title: Biomimetic graphitic carbon nitride nanoparticles for multiscale photomodulation and therapeutic intervention.
first_affiliation: Department of Biological and Chemical Engineering, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark.

abstract.text: Most organic matter on Earth originates from the conversion of solar energy through photosynthesis in chloroplasts. Here, drawing inspiration from photosynthesis, we develop hollow-sphere graphitic carbon nitride nanoparticles (hg-C3N4 NPs) that can modulate biological activity from subcellular processes to whole‑tissue function. The homogeneous hg-C3N4 NPs show responsiveness to light via both photoelectrochemical and photothermal mechanisms and can be spontaneously internalized with excellent cytocompatibility. Using a focusing laser, the hg-C3N4 NPs enable intracellular optical stimulation with subcellular resolution, inducing calcium-transient release in multiple cells and propagation in primary cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts. At the multicellular scale, optical pacing and synchronization of cardiomyocyte beating is readily achieved by light-emitting diodes. Further, we demonstrate that hg-C3N4 nanoparticles can be safely delivered and elicit measurable cortical and behavioural light responses in a model of advanced retinal degeneration. The application of hg-C3N4 NPs to porcine retinal tissue ex vivo confirms their modulation capability to directly activate retinal ganglion cell activity under light-emitting diode photostimulation. Taken together, hg-C3N4 NPs represent a versatile tool to address complex biomedical challenges through subcellular, intercellular and tissue-level photo-modulation.

title: Effects of Spatial Ambient Illumination on Pupil Diameter and Visual Acuity.
journal: Ophthalmic & physiological optics : the journal of the British College of Ophthalmic Opticians (Optometrists)
first_affiliation: Institute of Materials Science, VAST, Hanoi, Vietnam.

abstract.label: PURPOSE
abstract.text: Although chart luminance is carefully standardised in visual acuity (VA) testing, the luminance and spatial distribution of the surrounding illumination are less clearly defined. This study investigated how central luminance, peripheral field illumination and ambient room illumination influence pupil diameter and VA during small-field visual tasks.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A programmable light-emitting diode (LED) illumination system was developed to manipulate central chart luminance, peripheral field illumination and ambient room illumination surrounding a central Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart independently. VA and pupil diameter were measured in 201 participants under multiple lighting conditions. Relationships among illumination parameters, pupil diameter and VA were evaluated using paired comparisons and regression analysis.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Increasing central luminance from 20 to 640 cd/m² reduced mean pupil diameter from 5.93 to 3.61 mm and improved VA from 0.02 to -0.13 logMAR. At constant central luminance (160 cd/m²), increasing peripheral field extent and ambient illumination produced additional pupil constriction and modest improvements in VA. Changes in pupil diameter were significantly associated with changes in VA (r = 0.67, p < 0.001).

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The spatial distribution of illumination significantly influences pupil diameter and VA, even when central chart luminance remains unchanged. Both peripheral field illumination and ambient room lighting were associated with pupil constriction and modest improvements in VA. These findings highlight the importance of spatial illumination in visual performance and suggest that ambient lighting conditions should be considered in visual acuity assessment and visual environment design.

title: Three-year Comparative Efficacy and Safety of Repeated Low-level Red-light Therapy and Orthokeratology for Myopia Control in Children.
first_affiliation: Department of Ophthalmology, Shenzhen People's Hospital (The First Affiliated Hospital, Southern University of Science and Technology; The Second Clinical Medical College, Jinan University), Shenzhen, 518020, China.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Repeated low-level red-light therapy (RLRL) has emerged as a noninvasive intervention for myopia control in children. This study compared the 3-year efficacy and safety of RLRL and orthokeratology (OK).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This retrospective study included 86 children treated with RLRL (n = 40) or OK (n = 46). The RLRL group received two red-light treatment sessions daily and wore single-vision spectacles (SVS), whereas the OK group wore orthokeratology lenses overnight. Axial length (AL) and safety outcomes were assessed over 3 years. The measured baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: At 3 years, during active treatment, the mean change in AL from baseline was 0.00 ± 0.28 mm in the RLRL group and 0.45 ± 0.20 mm in the OK group (P < 0.001). Axial shortening, defined as an AL reduction of ≥ 0.05 mm from baseline, was more frequent in the RLRL group than in the OK group (40.00% vs. 2.17%). Complete myopia control, defined as axial elongation of < 0.10 mm/year, was also more frequent in the RLRL group at 3 years (82.5% vs. 37.0%). No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported in either group. One participant in the RLRL group showed reversible retinal hyperreflectivity on optical coherence tomography, without associated visual acuity loss or interruption of treatment.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: During active treatment, RLRL was associated with less axial elongation than OK over 3 years in this cohort. Both treatments showed acceptable safety profiles. Whether the observed between-group differences persist after treatment cessation remains unknown.

title: Effect of Photobiomodulation‑Based LED on Myopia Control in Children: An Exploratory Randomized Clinical Trial.
first_affiliation: Shanghai Eye Disease Prevention and Treatment Center/Eye Hospital of Tongji University, National Clinical Research Center for Eye Diseases, Shanghai, China.

abstract.label: INTRODUCTION
abstract.text: Laser-based repeated low-level red-light (RLRL) therapy may slow myopia progression, but evidence for lower-intensity noncoherent photobiomodulation-based light-emitting diode (PBM-LED) therapy remains limited. We evaluated its short-term efficacy and safety in children with myopia.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: In this single-center, double-masked, sham-controlled exploratory trial, 40 children aged 8-12 years were randomized 1:1 to PBM-LED or sham treatment twice daily for 3 months. Primary outcomes were axial length (AL) and cycloplegic spherical equivalent (SE).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: All participants completed follow-up. In eye-specific analyses, the intervention group showed less axial elongation, with significance only in the left eye at 3 months (difference, -0.056 mm; 95% confidence interval, -0.109 to -0.004; P = 0.036). Using participant-level means of both eyes, unadjusted 3-month differences were -0.059 mm for AL (P = 0.061) and 0.244 D for SE (P = 0.092); adjusted differences were not significant. Five eyes across both groups showed a 0.20-logMAR deterioration in uncorrected visual acuity at 3 months, but no eyes showed a 0.20-logMAR or greater decline in best-corrected visual acuity at 1 or 3 months. No serious adverse events or structural retinal abnormalities were observed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: PBM-LED showed a preliminary short-term treatment signal, but the small sample, unilateral nominal finding, nonsignificant adjusted participant-level analyses, visual-acuity changes, and short follow-up preclude definitive efficacy or long-term safety conclusions.
